rules.description: $cond: {if: a, then: b, else: c} and $cond: [a, b, c] are the same expression; the array form is canonical.
In a query predicate {f: {$eq: v}} matches the same documents as {f: v} unless v is a regular expression or a document whose first key is an operator; the short form is canonical.
In a query predicate f: /p/o, {$regex: /p/o}, {$regex: "p", $options: "o"} and {$regex: /p/, $options: "o"} are the same match; {$regex: "p", $options: "o"} with sorted options is canonical.

{f: {$gt: a, $lt: b}} is {$and: [{f: {$gt: a}}, {f: {$lt: b}}]}: each operator on a field is evaluated independently, so a one-field clause with several comparison operators is canonically an $and of one-operator clauses.

An expression operator that takes one argument accepts it bare or as a one-element argument list: {$isArray: ["$a"]} is {$isArray: "$a"}. The bare form is canonical; an argument that is itself an array literal is left wrapped.
The position of _id inside a projection does not change its output; _id first is canonical.
A top-level projection value of true or false is the same as 1 or 0; the number is canonical.
$unwind: "$p" is $unwind: {path: "$p"}; the document form is canonical.

An action block holds several commands of the same kind on one collection and the fixture holds one of them. The tool does not prove the alternatives equivalent: each use needs a reviewed justification in its declaration.

The top-level keys of an operator that takes only named arguments (for example $filter, $map, $dateToString, $bottomN, $fill, $graphLookup) may appear in any order; sorted keys are canonical. Nested values, including sort specifications, keep their order.
